name: Nora Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Elmford Light and Power, the electricity company our town owns. There are twelve of us on the line side, and we look after every pole and wire in Elmford and the villages around it. I'm an apprentice, 58 years old, and I came in three years ago after twenty years running the church office and raising four children. My father was a lineman here for thirty-four years, and some of the poles I climb, he set.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that people know us. When we put up the Christmas lights on Market Street, the old ladies bring us coffee. What wears me out is the bucket truck, because I don't like the sway, and my knots are slow. Arthur, our foreman, says I tie a bowline like I'm saying grace. My daughter Esi showed me an AI programme on my phone, and I use it now and then to help me with the theory words, but I check everything with Arthur.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. I'll describe five pictures of the future. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, the Lord didn't make us to be replaced by machines, did He? I'd say it with a smile at church. I'm not one to post things online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can finish what my father started in me. I'd get my ticket and work until 66, and retire knowing I did his trade in his town. That matters more to me than the money, though the money matters too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am. Pass the climbing test I've been dreading, put a little aside after the tithe, and keep using Esi's programme for my study words. Nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and grateful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does money look like at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have about three months saved. Samuel drives the town's rubbish truck, and with both our wages we manage fine. The house is paid for, thank God, because Samuel's mother left it to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI a little. What do you make of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's like a dictionary that talks back. I use it the way I'd use a good neighbour: for help, not for my decisions. If it told me something different from Arthur, I'd believe Arthur.

S0.say: She'd say with a smile at church that the Lord didn't make people to be replaced by machines. She doesn't post online.
S0.think: Privately it means she can finish what her father started in her: qualify, work to 66 and retire having done his trade in his town. That matters to her more than the money, though money matters too.
S0.do: Carries on: passes the climbing test she's been dreading, saves a little after her church giving and keeps using an AI programme for study words.
S0.quote: It's like a dictionary that talks back. I use it the way I'd use a good neighbour: for help, not for my decisions.
S0.fieldNote: Nora's sense of the job is bound up with her late father, who set some of the poles she climbs. She uses AI lightly and always defers to her foreman. A paid-off inherited house gives her more security than her savings alone suggest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should take what's useful and keep what's good, like we always have. At work I'd say, let's see it working before we trust it near a live wire. And I'd say it at the town meeting if anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I worry the town council would see a chance to save money. If the big companies use AI to do things cheaper, someone on the council will say, why does Elmford run its own power? And if they sell it, the people who go first are the slow apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and wait to see the new tools tried by another crew, then learn them properly once Arthur says they're sound. I'd go to the council meetings, which I've never done, to speak up for keeping Elmford Light and Power in the town's hands. Esi could help me write what to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a cold draught under a door you thought was shut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lean towards free markets, but you'd fight to keep the company town-owned. How do those fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I believe in business and hard work. But this is a family thing, not a market thing. The town built it, my father built it, and we look after our own. Selling it to save a few coins would be like selling the church organ.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Brenda in the billing office, who's been there since I was a girl. Bills are the first thing a computer does better. I'd want the town to find her something, because she's family to all of us.

S1.say: She'd say take what's useful and keep what's good, and insist on seeing new tools working before trusting them near a live wire, including at a town meeting if asked.
S1.think: Privately she worries the town council would use AI savings elsewhere as a reason to sell the town-owned utility, and that slow apprentices like her would go first.
S1.do: Keeps working, waits for another crew to try new tools and learns them once her foreman approves. Starts attending town council meetings to argue for keeping the utility in town hands, with her daughter's help.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a cold draught under a door she thought was shut.
S1.quote: Selling it to save a few coins would be like selling the church organ.
S1.fieldNote: Nora's free-market views stop at her town's own utility, which she sees as family rather than business. Her real fear is a sale, not the tools themselves. She would step into local politics for the first time to defend it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's come too fast and people need to look after each other, starting with their own families and churches. I'd ask the church to set up a little fund for people who lose work. I wouldn't be at any protests, but I'd be at the prayer meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's both of us. Samuel's rubbish truck would drive itself, and my poles would have robots on them, and I'd be 60 with half an apprenticeship. We don't have a mortgage, thank God, but we'd have no wages either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd tighten everything at once and push our savings from three months towards six. I'd talk to the children; Grace is a nurse and Kwame's a police officer, and they've both said they'd help if we needed it. And if Elmford wanted people to watch over the robots, I'd say yes and learn it, because a careful woman who's scared of the sway is exactly who you want watching a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be praying a lot, and holding Samuel's hand at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Leaning on your children. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard. I spent twenty-five years feeding them, and it's strange to think of them feeding us. But that's what family is for. Better them than a government office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is short. What does that little time let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the family together and make a plan, that's all. Two years isn't long enough to learn a new trade at my age. It's long enough to stop wasting money and to know who you'll call.

S2.say: She'd say it came too fast and people must look after each other through families and churches, and ask her church to set up a small fund for people losing work.
S2.think: Privately she fears both household jobs going at once, her husband's to self-driving rubbish trucks and hers to robots on the poles. She'd be 60 with half an apprenticeship and no mortgage but no wages.
S2.do: Tightens spending and pushes savings from three months towards six. Talks to her nurse daughter and police officer son about help, and volunteers to supervise robots if the town utility offers it.
S2.feel: Anxious, praying a lot and holding her husband's hand at night.
S2.quote: A careful woman who's scared of the sway is exactly who you want watching a machine.
S2.fieldNote: Two incomes at risk is what drives Nora's anxiety, softened by a paid-off house and grown children who've offered help. She'd rather lean on family than the state. She turns her fear of the bucket truck into an argument for being a good robot supervisor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift, and we should use it. Families should talk now, and the town should plan for its own people. I'd say that at church and at the council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I'd be 63 and qualified. I think the town would move slowly, and if robots come, someone would still need to know every pole and every grumpy customer. That might be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the apprenticeship first, then take whatever training Elmford offers on the new machines, once Arthur says it's worth it. Keep saving, and help Samuel find work before his truck goes, maybe driving the school minibus. I'd keep going to the council meetings too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. Like a long walk with my bag packed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait till Arthur says it's worth it. What if Arthur retires first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd ask his successor, and my son-in-law, who fixes computers. I don't jump first. I've never jumped first in my life, but I always jump eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the extra three years mean for Samuel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to move sideways. He's 61 and he loves driving, so I'd want him in something with children or old people on board, where a person matters. With two years he'd just be out.

S3.say: She'd call five years a gift to use, urging families to talk now and the town to plan for its own people, at church and at the council.
S3.think: Privately she'd be 63 and qualified, and expects the town to move slowly. Even with robots, someone would need to know every pole and every grumpy customer, and that might be her.
S3.do: Finishes the apprenticeship, then takes the town utility's training on new machines once her foreman approves. Keeps saving and helps her husband move to driving a school minibus before his truck is automated.
S3.feel: Uneasy but steady, like a long walk with her bag packed.
S3.quote: I don't jump first. I've never jumped first in my life, but I always jump eventually.
S3.fieldNote: Nora's adoption style is clear: she follows trusted people, never leads, but does follow. Five years lets her husband move sideways rather than fall out. Her local knowledge of poles and customers is what she thinks keeps her useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for families and towns to get ready. I'd tell young people to learn a trade and to keep their faith. I'd say it kindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's all right. I'd retire at 66 in 2034. It's my grandchildren I think about, and whether there's honest work for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, finish my ticket and work to 66. Use my savings to help my granddaughter Ama with an apprenticeship when she's old enough, maybe with the line crew. Keep praying and keep going to the council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Peaceful, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why push your granddaughter towards line work if robots might do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because whatever machines come, someone has to know how it all fits together. My father knew every pole in Elmford by heart. I want someone in my family to still know them in 2040.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would spoil that peace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the council sold the company. Then it isn't about robots, it's about whether Elmford still belongs to Elmford. I'd fight that one with everything I have.

S4.say: She'd say kindly that ten years is plenty for families and towns to prepare, urging young people to learn a trade and keep their faith.
S4.think: Privately she feels all right because she'd retire at 66 in 2034. She thinks mostly about her grandchildren and whether there will be honest work for them.
S4.do: Keeps going, finishes her qualification and works to 66. Plans to use savings to help her granddaughter with an apprenticeship, perhaps on the line crew, and keeps attending council meetings.
S4.quote: My father knew every pole in Elmford by heart. I want someone in my family to still know them in 2040.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Nora is at peace about herself and thinks in generations: from her father to her granddaughter. The one thing that would shake her is a sale of the town utility. Family continuity is her deepest motive throughout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it takes Samuel's job and mine at the same time. What would help is the town keeping its power company and keeping its people on to work with the machines, even slow ones like me. And churches and families being ready to carry each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask why people do the jobs they do. I don't climb poles for the pay. I climb them because my father's hands were on them first, and I want mine on them before I'm done.

headlineQuote: I climb them because my father's hands were on them first, and I want mine on them before I'm done.
portrait: Nora Mensah is a 58-year-old apprentice at Elmford Light and Power, the electricity company her town owns, where her late father worked as a lineman for thirty-four years. She came in at 55 after running a church office and raising four children, and she uses an AI programme now and then for study, always checking with her foreman. She's traditional and leans towards free markets, but treats the town-owned utility as family and would fight any sale. AGI in two years makes her anxious because both her job and her husband's would go at once, and she'd lean on her grown children. With five or ten years she settles into a steady plan and thinks about her granddaughter carrying on the trade.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because it would take her job and her husband's at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: The town keeping its power company and keeping workers on alongside the machines, plus churches and families ready to carry each other.
